newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-WOODS BACK INTO CONTENTION WITH RECORD ROUND.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-WOODS BACK INTO CONTENTION WITH RECORD ROUND.

text.p: Tiger Woods showed he cannot be ignored as he roared back into contention with a record-equalling 64 in the British Open on Saturday.
It left him on a three-under par 210 with the leaders yet to start their third round. He had begun the day four over par and 13 behind leader Darren Clarke of Northern Ireland.
The turning point came on the feared back nine when he picked up three shots in the space of two holes.

It began at the par five 542-yard 16th when he drove his second shot 281 yards to 15 feet from the pin and sank the putt for an eagle. But his birdie at the next, the par three 223-yard 17th, was even more spectacular.

His four iron tee shot was slightly wayward, going left of the green about 30 feet from the pin. With a slope in front him it left Woods a difficult second but he played a "bump and run" with a pitching wedge and it went in the hole to a huge roar from the gallery.

Woods admitted the shot did not go exactly as he planned. "To be honest I carried it past the spot I was looking at on the ground. I hit it just a fraction above it. But the slope was so severe it didn't really matter," he said.

A 10-foot putt on the 18th saved par and his 64 equalled the record for a British Open at Troon by Greg Norman in 1989. Norman's round was actually an eight under par but a slight modification to the course since then has reduced it to a par 71 from a par 72.
Woods described it as definitely one of the better rounds of his career. "Today was one of those days where I got a lot of breaks and made a lot of putts," he said.

The American world number one, who made a storming start with birdies on the first two holes, avoided the errors of the first two rounds which included a triple-bogey seven and a quadruple-bogey eight, but there was still drama, although of a different kind.
His drive on the seventh went right and hit a small girl in the crowd, bounced back and Woods made a birdie.
"I couldn't find her but I had the rules official give her the ball that hit her and apologised," he said.
Earlier, Woods had the spectators laughing when a baby started crying as he lined up on the third tee. He turned to the crowd and said: "Am I really playing that bad?"
Apart from his eagle, Woods had seven birdies and two dropped shots.

He described his recovery at the 11th where he had a bogey five as even more important than his eagle at the 16th. A bad bounce took the ball into the rough, a sandwedge only put it into some gorse but another sandwedge shot of 71 yards put him only four feet from the pin for a simple putt.

"Making bogeys like that are what saves rounds," he said. "If I had made a double (bogey) there, losing two shots on a day like today you feel like throwing some stuff away. Getting up and down from 71 yards definitely makes you feel good about yourself."
Asked if he thought he could still win, Woods replied: "You know, honestly I think I still can."
